entities.name: There's No Business Like Show Business

properties.plot_themes_description: The film explores how ambition and show-business dreams clash with family loyalty and faith, depicting sacrifice, addiction and the tensions between career goals and romantic commitments.
properties.description: There's No Business Like Show Business is a mid-1950s Technicolor musical directed by Walter Lang, released in early 1955 (often credited as a 1954 production). The all-star cast includes Ethel Merman, Marilyn Monroe, Donald O'Connor, Dan Dailey, Mitzi Gaynor, and Johnnie Ray performing Irving Berlin songs in grand CinemaScope numbers. The film follows a vaudeville family through ambition, romantic entanglements, and crises of faith, balancing sentimental family drama with lavish musical set pieces and rich orchestration. Visually sumptuous and emotionally warm, it celebrates classic show-business spectacle while probing family loyalty and personal sacrifice.

entities.name: Designing Woman

properties.plot_themes_description: Uses a mismatched marriage set against the worlds of fashion and Broadway to examine cultural clashes, gender expectations, and petty corruption in sport.
properties.description: Designing Woman (1957), directed by Vincente Minnelli and starring Gregory Peck, Lauren Bacall and Dolores Gray, is a witty romantic comedy. It follows a sportswriter and a fashion designer whose whirlwind marriage reveals deep incompatibilities and draws the writer into boxing-related corruption. The film mixes comedy of manners and show-business satire with polished CinemaScope visuals, colorful costuming, and strong supporting performances. Its tone is stylish and entertaining with a quietly melancholic undercurrent about marriage and identity.

entities.name: Last Tango in Paris

properties.plot_themes_description: The story examines how grief and desire collide in anonymous encounters that shift power, erode identity, and foster isolation and obsession.
properties.description: Last Tango in Paris (1972), directed by Bernardo Bertolucci and starring Marlon Brando, Maria Schneider and Maria Michi, is an art-house drama that uses eroticism and role-playing to interrogate grief, desire and power. The film follows a grieving American widower in Paris who enters an anonymous sexual relationship with a young Parisian, turning physical encounters into a tense psychological study. Through stark close-ups, improvisational performances and fraught power dynamics, the film explores trauma, identity and isolation, producing a raw, melancholic emotional effect.

entities.name: All That Heaven Allows

properties.plot_themes_description: The film examines how rigid social expectations and class-conscious hypocrisy in a midcentury suburban community punish personal desire and constrain a woman's pursuit of happiness.
properties.description: All That Heaven Allows (1955), directed by Douglas Sirk and starring Jane Wyman, Rock Hudson, and Agnes Moorehead, is a romantic drama told as a domestic melodrama. A well-to-do widow falls for a younger nurseryman and faces ostracism from her children and country-club peers, setting up a morally charged choice between love and social acceptance. The film pairs emotionally intense performances with lush, highly stylized visuals to examine class, conformity, and female autonomy. Its tone is bittersweet and emotionally affecting, framing personal longing against a critique of midcentury suburban hypocrisy.

entities.name: Sweet Charity

properties.plot_themes_description: Through showy musical numbers and intimate character moments, the story explores longing for connection, the persistence of hope after disappointment, and personal resilience in a harsh urban world.
properties.description: Sweet Charity (1969), directed by Bob Fosse and starring Shirley MacLaine with John McMartin and Ricardo Montalban, is a film musical that follows a hopeful taxi dancer in New York as she pursues love and a better life. Built around Cy Coleman’s songs and Fosse’s distinctive choreography, the film mixes buoyant production numbers with bittersweet, character-driven drama. Themes of vulnerability, resilience, and longing are threaded through both comic and poignant set pieces to produce an emotionally affecting showbiz fable.

properties.plot_themes_description: The story examines the ethics and human cost of scientific experimentation, how sudden cognitive change affects identity and relationships, and the experience of isolation, loss, and memory decline.
properties.description: Charly (1968), directed by Ralph Nelson and starring Cliff Robertson, Claire Bloom and Lilia Skala, is a dramatic literary adaptation of Flowers for Algernon that blends romantic and science-fiction elements. It follows a mentally disabled man who undergoes an experimental procedure that raises his intelligence to genius levels, altering his relationships and sense of self. The film explores ethical questions about human experimentation, the loneliness of sudden cognitive change, and the emotional costs that follow. Its tone is poignant and ultimately tragic, anchored by a central performance that traces both wonder and loss.

properties.plot_themes_description: Through family conversations and confrontations, the story explores interracial relationships, societal prejudice, personal conscience, and the tensions between liberal ideals and private fears.
properties.description: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967), directed by Stanley Kramer and starring Spencer Tracy, Katharine Hepburn, and Sidney Poitier, is a comedy-drama about a liberal San Francisco family whose values are tested when their daughter arrives engaged to a Black physician. The film unfolds largely over one day and a single dinner, using intimate, dialogue-rich scenes to examine racism, family loyalty, and the clash between principle and fear. Noted for its powerful performances and a climactic paternal monologue, the movie balances moments of gentle humor with serious social commentary. Its tone is earnest and emotionally affecting, inviting viewers to reflect on love, acceptance, and social change.

entities.name: Play It Again, Sam

properties.plot_themes_description: The film explores how nostalgia and imagined ideals complicate the process of recovering from heartbreak, while friendship and awkward courtship become means of personal reinvention.
properties.description: Play It Again, Sam (1972), directed by Herbert Ross and starring Woody Allen, Diane Keaton and Tony Roberts, is a romantic comedy adapted from a stage play. The story follows a film critic who, devastated by his wife’s departure, attempts to restart his love life with the help of friends and his imagined idol, Humphrey Bogart. The film blends broad comic set pieces with tender, character-driven moments and a fond cinematic nostalgia for classic Hollywood. Its tone is affectionate and gently wistful, exploring themes of heartbreak, identity and the gap between fantasy and real relationships.

properties.plot_themes_description: Through a romantic farce set in the theatre world, the story interrogates class divides, the construction of identity, and how money and fame shape personal relationships and artistic life.
properties.description: Let's Make Love (1960), directed by George Cukor and produced by Jerry Wald, is a romantic musical comedy starring Marilyn Monroe, Yves Montand and Tony Randall. Set around an off‑Broadway revue, the story follows a wealthy industrialist who masquerades as an actor to get close to the show's leading lady, leading to comic misunderstandings, musical performances and a developing romance. The picture pairs glossy studio production numbers and star turns with a light satirical inquiry into class, celebrity and authenticity. Its tone is playful and charming, punctuated by bittersweet notes about money and identity.

properties.plot_themes_description: The story examines how 1950s social expectations and workplace power dynamics force women to choose between romantic relationships and professional ambitions, producing personal sacrifice and interpersonal conflict.
properties.description: The Best of Everything (1959), directed by Jean Negulesco and starring Hope Lange, Stephen Boyd and Suzy Parker with Joan Crawford in a key supporting role, is a drama-romance adapted from Rona Jaffe’s novel. The film follows several young secretaries at a New York publishing firm as they confront affairs, pregnancy, workplace manipulation, and the tension between career ambition and romantic desire. Presented as a glossy 1950s melodrama, it highlights fashion, office culture and fraught female relationships while interrogating midcentury gender expectations. The overall tone is emotionally charged and bittersweet, balancing escapist glamour with sobering consequences.
